{{Probability distribution

|  type       =density

|  pdf_caption=Example density curves for the PERT probability distribution
|  cdf_image  =PERT cdf examples.jpg
| cdf_caption=Example cumulative distribution curves for the PERT probability distribution
|  parameters =<math>b>a\,</math> [[real number|(real)]] <br><math>c>b\,</math> [[real number|(real)]]
|  support    =<math>x \in [a,c]\,</math>
|  pdf        =<math>\frac{(x-a)^{\alpha-1}(c-x)^{\beta-1}} {\Beta(\alpha,\beta)(c-a)^{\alpha+\beta-1}} </math>
where 
<math>\alpha = \frac{4b+c-5a} {c-a} = 1 + 4 \frac{b-a}{c-a}</math>
<math>\beta = \frac{5c-a-4b} {c-a} = 1 + 4 \frac{c-b}{c-a}</math>
|  cdf        = <math>I_z(\alpha,\beta)</math>
(the regularized [[incomplete beta function]]) with <math>z = (x-a)/(c-a)</math>
| mean   = <math>\operatorname{E}[X] = \frac{a+4b+c}{6}=\mu</math>
|median = <math>I_{\frac{1}{2}}^{[-1]}(\alpha,\beta)(c-a) + a </math> 
<math>\approx a + (c-a) \frac{\alpha-1/3}{\alpha+\beta - 2/3} = \frac{a + 6 b + c}{8}</math>
| mode     = <math>b</math>
| variance = <math>\operatorname{var}[X] = \frac{(\mu-a)(c-\mu)}{7}</math>
| skewness = <math>\frac{2\,(\beta-\alpha)\sqrt{\alpha+\beta+1}}{(\alpha+\beta+2)\sqrt{\alpha\beta}}</math>
| kurtosis = <math>\frac{6[(\alpha - \beta)^2 (\alpha +\beta + 1) - \alpha \beta (\alpha + \beta + 2)]}{\alpha \beta (\alpha + \beta + 2) (\alpha + \beta + 3)}</math>
| entropy  = <math>\ln(\Beta(\alpha,\beta)(c-a))-(\alpha-1)\psi(\alpha)-(\beta-1)\psi(\beta)+4\psi(6)</math>
}}
In [[probability]] and [[statistics]], the '''[[Program evaluation and review technique|PERT]] distributions''' are a family of [[continuous probability distribution]]s defined by the minimum (''a''), most likely (''b'') and maximum (''c'') values that a variable can take. It is a transformation of the four-parameter [[beta distribution]] with an additional assumption that its [[expected value]] is

:<math> \mu = \frac{a+4b+c} 6.</math>

The mean of the distribution is therefore defined as the weighted average of the minimum, most likely and maximum values that the variable may take, with four times the weight applied to the most likely value.
This assumption about the mean was first proposed in Clark, 1962<ref>Clark CE (1962) The PERT model for the distribution of an activity. Operations Research 10, pp. 405406</ref> for estimating the effect of uncertainty of task durations on the outcome of a project schedule being evaluated using the [[program evaluation and review technique]], hence its name. The mathematics of the distribution resulted from the authors' desire to make the standard deviation equal to about 1/6 of the range.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vosesoftware.com/riskwiki/PERTdistribution.php |title=PERT distribution |publisher=Vose Software |date=May 2, 2017 |access-date=July 16, 2017}}</ref><ref>Continuous Univariate Distributions - 2nd Ed (1995). Johnson K, Kotz S and Balakkrishnan N.  (Section 25.4)</ref> 
The PERT distribution is widely used in [[Risk Analysis|risk analysis]]<ref>Project Management Body of Knowledge: 5th Ed (2013).  Project Management Institute  Chapter 6</ref> to represent the uncertainty of the value of some quantity where one is relying on subjective estimates, because the three parameters defining the distribution are intuitive to the estimator. The PERT distribution is featured in most simulation software tools.

==Comparison with the triangular distribution==

[[File:Triangle v PERT distributions.jpg|thumb|Comparing density curves for the PERT and triangular probability distributions]]

The PERT distribution offers an alternative<ref>Simulation Modeling and Analysis (2000). Law AM and Kelton WD. Section 6.11</ref> to using the [[triangular distribution]] which takes the same three parameters. The PERT distribution has a smoother shape than the [[triangular distribution]]. The triangular distribution has a mean equal to the average of the three parameters:

:<math> \mu = \frac{a+b+c} 3</math>

which (unlike PERT) places equal emphasis on the extreme values which are usually less-well known than the most likely value, and is therefore less reliable. The triangular distribution also has an angular shape that does not match the smoother shape that typifies subjective knowledge.

==The modified-PERT distribution==

[[File:Modified PERT example pdfs.jpg|thumb|Comparing density curves for the modified PERT distributions with different weights]]

The PERT distribution assigns very small probability to extreme values, particularly to the extreme furthest away from the most likely value if the distribution is strongly skewed.<ref>Business Risk and Simulation Modelling in Practice (2015). M Rees. Section 9.1.8</ref><ref>Risk Analysis – a Quantitative Guide: 3rd Ed. (2008) Vose D</ref> The Modified PERT distribution <ref>{{cite web|title=Modified Pert Simulation|url=http://www.greatsolutions.com.br/images/BetaEng.pdf/|access-date=July 14, 2017|author=Paulo Buchsbaum|website=Greatsolutions.com.br|date=June 9, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181223183535/http://greatsolutions.com.br/images/BetaEng.pdf|archive-date=December 23, 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> was proposed to provide more control on how much probability is assigned to tail values of the distribution. The modified-PERT introduces a fourth parameter <math> \gamma,</math> that controls the weight of the most likely value in the determination of the mean:

:<math> \mu = \frac{a+\gamma b+c}{\gamma+2}</math>

Typically, values of between 2 and 3.5 are used for <math> \gamma,</math> and have the effect of flattening the density curve; the unmodified PERT would use <math>\gamma=4</math>. This is useful for highly skewed distributions where the distances <math>(b-a),</math> and <math>(c-b),</math> are of very different sizes.

The modified-PERT distribution has been implemented in several simulation packages and programming languages:
* ModelRisk<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vosesoftware.com/riskwiki/ModifiedPERTdistribution.php |title=Modified PERT distribution |publisher=Vose Software |date=May 2, 2017 |access-date=July 16, 2017}}</ref> – risk analysis add-in for [[Microsoft Excel|Excel]].
* [[Primavera (software)|Primavera]] risk analysis – project risk analysis simulation tool.
* Tamara<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vosesoftware.com/riskwiki/DistributionsusedinTamara.php |title=Probability distributions used in Tamara |publisher=Vose Software |date=May 2, 2017 |access-date=July 16, 2017}}</ref> – project risk analysis simulation tool.
* [[Wolfram Mathematica]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/PERTDistribution.html.en |title=PERTDistribution—Wolfram Language Documentation |website=Reference.wolfram.com |access-date=July 16, 2017}}</ref> – mathematical symbolic computation program.
* [[R (programming language)]]: ''mc2d'' package.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mc2d/mc2d.pdf#Rfn.pert.1 |title = Package ‘mc2d’|date= March 6, 2017|access-date=December 16, 2020}}</ref>
* [[Python (programming language)]]: ''pertdist'' package.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pypi.org/project/pertdist/ |title = PertDist|date= December 6, 2020|access-date=January 5, 2021}}</ref>
